He joins George and Harris in prescribing themselves a boating holiday and recounts the expedition, its digressions, and earlier disasters with a mixture of observation and self-justification.
characters.name: J.

characters.description: J.'s friend, who works at a bank and supports the plan for a restorative holiday. He cannot leave work with the others and arranges to join them at Weybridge. George is confident about practical matters and music, though his results regularly fail to support that confidence.
characters.name: George

characters.description: The third man in the proposed holiday party. Harris readily diagnoses himself as overworked and contributes firm views on food, camping, and the division of labor. He tends to direct work from a comfortable position and is capable of becoming lost even when certain he knows the way.
characters.name: William Samuel Harris

characters.description: J.'s fox terrier, whose appearance suggests innocence more than his conduct does. Montmorency is delighted by fights, cats, and opportunities to obstruct a task, and the three men treat his reactions as a fourth vote in their discussions.
characters.name: Montmorency

characters.description: J.'s housekeeper, who wakes the party on the morning they mean to depart. The men have misread the time and initially believe they have been roused in the middle of the night.
characters.name: Mrs Poppets

characters.description: J.'s uncle, remembered for attempting to hang a picture without professional help. The small job occupies the entire household as he loses tools, injures himself, damages the wall, and continues insisting that the task is simple.
characters.name: Uncle Podger

characters.description: A friend who asks J. to take two strong-smelling cheeses from Liverpool to London. The favor makes J. unpopular with fellow railway passengers and creates further trouble when the cheeses reach Tom's household.
characters.name: Tom

characters.description: An attendant at the Hampton Court maze. Harris eventually encounters him after trying to guide a growing group of visitors to the exit; the keeper enters the maze to lead them out and becomes confused as well.
characters.name: The maze keeper

characters.description: An elderly angler at a riverside inn who claims that the enormous trout in a display case is his catch. Several other visitors tell J. and George incompatible stories of catching the same fish.
characters.name: The old fisherman

recaps.ending: Rain settles over the river after the party reaches Oxford and turns the return journey into a cold, dispiriting exercise. The men initially insist that they will complete the holiday, but everything is wet, the scenery is obscured, and another evening under canvas promises no relief. At Pangbourne they finally abandon the plan. They leave the boat to be collected and take the train to London, where a substantial meal in a restaurant restores their spirits. From the comfort of dry clothes and full stomachs, George, Harris, and J. agree that ending early was wise. Montmorency's response shows equal satisfaction. The narrative closes with the dog apparently grateful that the three men have returned from the river alive, ending the expedition with relief rather than arrival at its planned destination.
recaps.in_short: Convinced that they are ill from overwork, J., George, and Harris prescribe themselves a fortnight's boating holiday on the Thames, accompanied by J.'s fox terrier Montmorency. J. and Harris start from Kingston and collect George at Weybridge. Their upstream journey becomes a sequence of mishaps involving packing, camping, cooking, towing, locks, other boats, and their own exaggerated confidence. J. fills the voyage with memories of earlier domestic and boating failures and with reflections on the history of the river. The friends pass Hampton Court, Marlow, Reading, and other towns, create an improvised stew, quarrel with a tin of pineapple, misuse George's banjo, and discover that a celebrated trout is made of plaster. They reach Oxford, but continuous rain ruins the return trip. At Pangbourne they leave the boat and take a train to London, where dinner and dry surroundings convince all four travelers that abandoning the holiday was their best decision.

recaps.text: J., George, and Harris spend an evening comparing their health and conclude that each is seriously overworked. J. has recently consulted a medical book and recognized in himself almost every illness it describes, but his doctor has prescribed ordinary food, sleep, and exercise. The friends decide they need a holiday. A sea voyage is considered and rejected after stories of seasickness, and they choose instead to row and camp along the Thames. They plan a route from Kingston toward Oxford, include J.'s fox terrier Montmorency, reduce their equipment to supposed essentials, and divide the responsibilities with more enthusiasm than precision.

Packing turns into a prolonged contest between the men's confidence and their disorganization, with Montmorency repeatedly interfering. J. and Harris eventually carry the luggage to Waterloo and struggle to identify the correct train before reaching Kingston. George must work that day and will join them later. Once afloat, they move upstream past familiar places that prompt J.'s historical reflections and personal stories. At Hampton Court, Harris recounts entering the maze certain that he could guide other visitors out; his party only grew as more lost people joined it, and even the keeper had difficulty rescuing them. J. and Harris continue toward the meeting with George.

George joins at Weybridge, and the complete party settles into the routines of rowing, steering, towing, camping, and arguing over who has done the most work. They encounter the unwritten rules and mutual irritations of the river, particularly the conflict between small boats and steam launches. J.'s earlier experiences supply examples of tow ropes causing chaos and inexperienced boaters making simple maneuvers dangerous. The men repeatedly condemn in others the same behavior they excuse in themselves. Even so, fair weather, food, and the river make the expedition pleasant between mishaps.

The first night under canvas requires a difficult struggle with the boat's covering before the men can eat and sleep. In the morning, small tasks such as bathing and finding a toothbrush become ordeals. The travelers pass places associated with the history of the Thames, including the country around Runnymede, while J. alternates between serious reflection and stories of the party's incompetence. Harris becomes separated from the others during one episode and gives an elaborate account of fighting swans. Later, the men discover that possessing a sealed tin of pineapple is useless when nobody has packed a tin opener.

Continuing upstream, the friends pass Marlow and other river towns, complain about steam launches, and contribute their own share of inconvenience to traffic. George attempts to learn the banjo, but neither his companions nor the people along the bank welcome the practice. Supper one evening becomes an improvised stew made from the available food, with Montmorency offering a dead water rat that the cooks decline. Further recollections cover the hazards of punting and sailing, activities that J. presents as simple only before describing how easily they go wrong. The crew nevertheless continues toward Oxford.

A steam launch that has been impatient with slower boats is eventually required to tow J.'s party, reversing their position in the river's usual quarrel. Fishing stories then become the chief subject. At an inn, an old man claims to have caught the enormous trout displayed in a glass case; after he leaves, several other men separately take credit for it. George tries to inspect the celebrated fish and knocks the case down. The trout breaks apart and proves to be plaster, exposing all the proud accounts as inventions. The travelers reach the later part of their route as the weather begins to threaten the easy pleasure of the voyage.

The party reaches Oxford and begins the downstream return, but persistent rain transforms the river. Wet clothes, cold meals, and obscured scenery destroy their enthusiasm. They try to maintain the principle that a holiday should be completed as planned, then abandon it at Pangbourne rather than spend another miserable night under canvas. The boat is left to be collected and the men take a train to London. A large restaurant dinner restores their good humor, and they congratulate themselves on the wisdom of retreat. Montmorency is equally content to be home, closing the journey with all four travelers happier about comfort than disappointed by the unfinished route.

characters.description: The first-person narrator and one of three London friends who persuade themselves that overwork has damaged their health. He proposes a boating holiday on the Thames and records the journey, frequently interrupting it with memories of earlier mishaps and reflections on the places they pass.
characters.name: J.

characters.description: J.'s friend, who works at a bank and agrees that the group needs a holiday. Because he must remain at work on the first day, he plans to meet the others farther up the Thames. He approaches camping, cooking, and music with confidence that is not always justified.
characters.name: George

characters.description: The third man in the holiday party. Harris is practical enough to help plan the trip but often avoids work while explaining how it ought to be done. He can become confused by simple tasks and believes his comic singing gives more pleasure than his companions think it does.
characters.name: William Samuel Harris

characters.description: J.'s small fox terrier and the fourth member of the boating party. Montmorency has an energetic interest in fights, noise, and anything that interferes with orderly packing. The men treat him as a companion with strong opinions about their plans.
characters.name: Montmorency

characters.description: J.'s housekeeper, who wakes the men on the morning of their departure after they have misunderstood the time. Her intervention keeps the holiday from beginning even later than it does.
characters.name: Mrs Poppets

characters.description: J.'s uncle, remembered as a man who turned hanging a picture into a household emergency. He insisted on doing every part himself while directing everyone else to fetch tools and clean up the damage.
characters.name: Uncle Podger

characters.description: An elderly man encountered near the end of the journey who claims that an enormous trout displayed in a riverside inn is his own catch. His story proves to be one of several competing accounts attached to the same famous fish.
characters.name: The old fisherman

recaps.ending: Persistent rain changes the holiday from an inconvenience into a thoroughly wet ordeal. The men make one last attempt to continue, but cold food, damp clothes, and the prospect of another night under canvas defeat their determination. They leave the boat to be collected, take a train back to London, and finish the evening with a substantial meal in a restaurant. Warm, dry, and well fed, they agree that abandoning the river was the sensible decision. Montmorency's contented response confirms the verdict. The journey therefore ends before the planned destination, with the friends pleased by their adventure but even more pleased to have returned to ordinary comfort.
recaps.in_short: J., George, Harris, and J.'s dog Montmorency decide that a boating holiday will cure the illnesses the three men imagine they have. They plan to row up the Thames from Kingston, with George joining after work, but packing and departure immediately reveal how poorly their confidence matches their practical skill. On the river they struggle with camping equipment, cooking, towing, weather, and one another, while J. recalls earlier disasters involving boats, household jobs, and travel. They pass historic towns and riverside landmarks, encounter boastful anglers and impatient steam launches, and repeatedly turn minor tasks into confusion. The trip remains enjoyable while the weather is fair, but sustained rain eventually leaves everything wet and the party miserable. They abandon the boat, return to London by train, and celebrate their retreat with a large dinner, Montmorency plainly approving the decision.

recaps.text: J., George, and Harris compare their many supposed illnesses and conclude that they are suffering from overwork. They decide that a holiday together is the cure. After rejecting a sea voyage and discussing the difficulties of sleeping outdoors, they settle on a boating trip up the Thames. J.'s fox terrier Montmorency is included in the party. Their planning already exposes the pattern of the expedition: each man has firm opinions about what the others should do, and all three underestimate the work involved.

The friends reduce an impractical packing list, then make a disorderly job of putting their supplies together. Montmorency contributes by getting in the way. On departure day J. and Harris travel to Kingston with the luggage while George remains at his bank job and plans to join them later. Finding the correct train and moving their equipment are harder than expected, but the boat is finally loaded and the holiday begins. Along the way, J. recalls other examples of simple domestic work expanding into chaos, including Uncle Podger's attempt to hang a picture.

J. and Harris make their way along the river, passing places whose histories prompt J. to mix observation with comic memories. Harris recounts becoming lost in the Hampton Court maze while trying to guide other visitors out. George joins the boat as arranged, completing the human crew. The friends camp, cook, row, and tow with uneven success. Encounters with other river users reveal an elaborate etiquette that nobody consistently follows, and the men's certainty about their own competence repeatedly survives evidence to the contrary.

The journey continues through locks and riverside towns. Everyday problems dominate: opening food without the right tool, arranging meals, keeping the boat moving, and deciding whose turn it is to work. The party is annoyed by steam launches when rowing, then discovers how useful one can be when they need a tow. J.'s recollections of previous boating expeditions add further examples of fouled ropes, misguided towing, and confident beginners losing control. Despite their complaints, the friends continue upstream and enjoy the river when conditions cooperate.

Near the later stages of the trip, stories about fishing become another test of credibility. At an inn, several men independently claim to have caught the same enormous trout displayed in a glass case. When George accidentally breaks the case, the celebrated fish proves not to be a preserved catch at all. Meanwhile the weather worsens. Rain soaks the boat, their clothing, and their enthusiasm, and the prospect of continuing to live under wet canvas becomes increasingly unattractive.

The men try to persist through the rain but finally admit that the holiday has ceased to be enjoyable. Rather than complete the intended route, they arrange for the boat to be collected and take the train back to London. There they exchange damp discomfort for warmth and a generous restaurant meal. From the safety of dry clothes, they congratulate themselves on making the right choice. Montmorency also appears relieved, and the unfinished river journey closes as a successful retreat to comfort rather than a triumph of endurance.

characters.description: The narrator, a Londoner given to diagnosing himself with alarming illnesses and turning ordinary inconveniences into elaborate reflections. He joins his friends in proposing a restorative river holiday and records the journey through comic digressions, memories, and observations.
characters.name: J.

characters.description: A bank clerk and one of Jerome's two companions on the Thames trip. Practical in some matters but no less susceptible than his friends to laziness, misplaced confidence, and mishap, he must remain at work until the party is ready to leave.
characters.name: George

characters.description: Jerome's other human traveling companion. Harris is hearty, opinionated, and convinced of his competence, qualities repeatedly tested by the practical demands of boating and camping.
characters.name: Harris

characters.description: Jerome's small fox terrier and the fourth member of the expedition. Energetic, inquisitive, and eager to treat other animals as challenges, he complicates preparations while appearing entirely satisfied with his contribution.
characters.name: Montmorency

characters.description: The woman who keeps house for Jerome. Her practical response to the friends' late-night discussion helps bring their first evening of holiday planning to a close.
characters.name: Mrs. Poppets

characters.description: A relative remembered by Jerome as a model of bustling self-confidence. When he undertakes a simple household task, he directs everyone around him and turns the job into a prolonged family disturbance.
characters.name: Uncle Podger

recaps.ending: Persistent rain defeats the travelers' remaining enthusiasm for outdoor life. After enduring wet clothes, a cheerless meal, and an increasingly miserable boat, Jerome, George, and Harris abandon the Thames journey before completing their planned route. They leave the boat to be collected and take a train back to London, where dry surroundings, a substantial supper, and familiar city comforts restore their spirits. Harris closes the holiday by expressing gratitude that they returned when they did. The expedition has not proved the clean, health-giving escape imagined at the outset, but its succession of errors, digressions, and shared discomforts has become the substance of the friends' adventure.
recaps.in_short: Jerome, George, and Harris decide that overwork and imagined illness require a boating holiday on the Thames, accompanied by Jerome's terrier, Montmorency. Their preparations immediately expose their talent for making simple jobs difficult. Traveling upstream from Kingston, they pass historic places, struggle with camping equipment, cooking, towing, locks, weather, and one another, while Jerome repeatedly interrupts the journey with memories and reflections about river life. Moments of beauty and companionship alternate with rain, hunger, damaged provisions, and comic failures of expertise. Near Oxford, prolonged bad weather removes the last pleasure from the expedition. The three men give up the boat, return to London by train, and celebrate with a comfortable meal, relieved to exchange their supposedly healthy outdoor holiday for the conveniences of the city.

recaps.text: Jerome, George, and Harris spend an evening comparing their poor health. Jerome is especially prone to discovering symptoms after reading medical information, while each man believes that rest and a change of scene are needed. They reject a sea voyage and settle on a boating holiday along the Thames, with Jerome's dog Montmorency included. The friends debate whether to camp in the open or sleep at inns, eventually choosing a covered boat that offers some shelter without giving up the idea of outdoor life. They prepare lists of what to take, steadily reducing an impractical inventory to essentials. Their confidence in organizing the expedition recalls Jerome's Uncle Podger, whose attempts to manage a simple household task create far more work for everyone around him.

Packing proves as disorderly as the planning. George and Harris repeatedly repack the food while Montmorency gets among the contents, and ordinary items become difficult to locate or handle. The party reaches the river and begins its upstream journey from Kingston. As they pass familiar riverside places, Jerome mixes observations of the present with stories about history and earlier outings. The friends encounter the recurring complications of crowded water, uncertain steering, and towlines. Harris's confidence is particularly vulnerable to experience: a visit to the Hampton Court maze becomes a memory of his leading an increasingly large and frustrated group without finding the way out. The holiday has begun, but the contrast between the men's ideal of calm river life and their actual competence is already clear.

The travelers continue upstream through locks and busy stretches of river, observing the habits and vanities of other boaters while displaying many of the same weaknesses themselves. Towing creates tangles, delays, and arguments about who is working. Their first attempts at settled camp life are equally demanding: putting up the canvas, preparing food, and keeping possessions dry require more effort than expected. A plan to make Irish stew turns into a general use for assorted provisions, with Montmorency offering an addition that the cooks decline. The friends do eventually eat and rest, and quiet stretches of river sometimes fulfill the peaceful promise that brought them away from London. Yet each success is surrounded by anecdotes of accidents and by the party's tendency to treat avoidable problems as acts of fate.

Moving farther up the Thames, Jerome reflects on places associated with Magna Carta, royal history, and earlier life beside the river. The party's practical troubles continue. Finding water, dealing with the kettle, arranging meals, and keeping control of the boat all produce fresh confusion. Harris attempts to cook scrambled eggs with more confidence than success, and George's relation to work remains largely theoretical. Encounters with steam launches and other river users encourage the men to condemn inconsiderate behavior, though they readily enjoy inconveniencing boats they dislike. The journey remains pleasurable in clear weather, with old towns and changing scenery giving it shape, but fatigue and minor disagreements increasingly qualify the friends' romantic expectations.

The men continue toward Oxford, passing Reading and other upper-river towns while Jerome adds stories about fishing, inns, and the unreliability of impressive local tales. At one inn, a celebrated preserved trout becomes the center of several incompatible claims before an accident exposes its true nature. The weather then deteriorates. Rain soaks the travelers and their belongings, the covered boat becomes cramped and uncomfortable, and songs and conversation fail to sustain their spirits. Faced with more wet days, Jerome, George, and Harris abandon the planned remainder of the trip. They arrange for the boat to be collected, take the train back to London, and restore themselves with a generous supper in warm, dry surroundings. Harris declares their return a fortunate decision, ending the expedition in contented relief rather than triumph over the river.

characters.description: A Trenton apprehension agent whose growing experience has not made her work predictable. She is assigned to recover a beloved local merchant, putting her income and professional obligation against the Burg's conviction that the man deserves protection rather than arrest.
characters.name: Stephanie Plum

characters.description: A Trenton vice cop with a long and unresolved personal history with Stephanie. He understands the drug activity behind the new deaths and has police resources Stephanie lacks, but their attraction and mutual competitiveness keep cooperation from becoming simple.
characters.name: Joe Morelli

characters.description: Vinnie's most accomplished apprehension agent and Stephanie's principal professional mentor. He supplies training, backup, and occasional work beyond her own files, while expecting her to keep functioning under pressure rather than waiting to be rescued.
characters.name: Ranger

characters.description: A former street worker employed in Vinnie's office who increasingly acts as Stephanie's field partner. Lula brings local knowledge, confidence, and enthusiasm to surveillance and apprehensions, even when her methods are as improvised as Stephanie's.
characters.name: Lula

characters.description: The longtime proprietor of an ice-cream and candy store in the Burg, regarded by generations of neighborhood families as kind, respectable, and harmless. He fails to appear in court on a concealed-weapon charge, and the bond makes him Stephanie's target despite the community's hostility to anyone pursuing him.
characters.name: Moses Bedemier

characters.description: Stephanie's cousin and the owner of the bail-bond agency. He requires her to recover Uncle Mo because the bond is at risk, but contributes little when the assignment makes her unpopular across the neighborhood.
characters.name: Vinnie Plum

characters.description: The office manager at Vincent Plum Bail Bonds. She provides the file on Uncle Mo, keeps track of Stephanie's other cases, and serves as a dependable source of neighborhood information when the Burg closes ranks.
characters.name: Connie Rosolli

characters.description: Stephanie's former schoolmate and the woman with whom Stephanie's ex-husband was unfaithful. Now trying bounty work herself, Joyce approaches the occupation as a competition and is willing to interfere with Stephanie's cases for money or advantage.
characters.name: Joyce Barnhardt

characters.description: Stephanie's outspoken grandmother, always interested in arrests, weapons, and neighborhood scandal. She knows Uncle Mo by reputation and reflects the Burg's initial disbelief that the candy-store owner could be connected to serious danger.
characters.name: Grandma Mazur

characters.description: Stephanie's mother, who measures her daughter's increasingly hazardous work against the stable family life she wishes Stephanie would choose. She provides meals, warnings, and a home base while trying to contain Grandma Mazur's enthusiasm.
characters.name: Helen Plum

characters.description: Stephanie's father, a retired postal worker who generally responds to the upheaval created by Stephanie and Grandma Mazur with silence and attempts to preserve his routine.
characters.name: Frank Plum

characters.description: A Trenton police officer related to Stephanie by marriage. He remains a cautious law-enforcement contact, able to confirm some developments while unwilling to turn police files over to a civilian apprehension agent.
characters.name: Eddie Gazarra

recaps.ending: Stephanie's pursuit finally separates Uncle Mo's public reputation from what he has been doing in secret. Moses Bedemier has been carrying out a vigilante campaign against local drug dealers, making himself the killer behind the bodies that accumulated during the fugitive search. The neighborhood's affection for the candy-store owner allowed him to move with little suspicion and made witnesses resist Stephanie, but the evidence and the final confrontation expose him. Mo dies when the confrontation turns violent, ending both the bond pursuit and the killings. Stephanie completes the case without the satisfaction of returning a living fugitive and with little gratitude from people who preferred the familiar public image. Lula has become a genuine field partner, Ranger continues to treat Stephanie as a developing professional, and Morelli remains both an investigative ally and a personal complication. Stephanie's standing as a bounty hunter is firmer, even though the case demonstrates that her own neighborhood can be one of the hardest places for her to work.
recaps.in_short: Stephanie Plum's next important fugitive is Moses Bedemier, known throughout the Burg as Uncle Mo, the trusted owner of a candy and ice-cream shop. He skips court on a concealed-weapon charge, but neighbors obstruct Stephanie because they cannot believe he is dangerous. As she searches with help from Lula, Ranger, and Joe Morelli, dead drug dealers appear and the case expands beyond a routine bond recovery. Joyce Barnhardt complicates the work by competing for apprehensions, while the Burg's loyalty keeps useful information hidden. The evidence eventually shows that Mo's harmless public identity concealed a vigilante campaign: he has been killing people he regarded as drug threats to the neighborhood. Stephanie confronts him, and Mo dies when the encounter turns violent. The exposure ends the killings and closes the bond case, leaving Stephanie more established professionally but newly aware that community approval can conceal danger as effectively as fear.

recaps.text: Previously: Stephanie Plum became an apprehension agent after unemployment forced her to seek work from her cousin Vinnie's bail-bond office. Ranger has trained her in the practical basics, Lula has moved from witness to office employee and field companion, and Trenton vice cop Joe Morelli remains an intermittent ally and unresolved former lover. Stephanie has completed two major cases, but she still works through persistence, family and neighborhood contacts, and improvised plans rather than polished technique. The job now pays her bills, and recovering Vinnie's clients is an occupation rather than a temporary emergency.

Stephanie is assigned to recover Moses Bedemier, universally known in the Burg as Uncle Mo. The elderly owner of a candy and ice-cream store failed to appear on a concealed-weapon charge. On paper he is a straightforward bond fugitive; in neighborhood memory he is the trusted shopkeeper who served generations of children. Residents refuse to help Stephanie and condemn the pursuit as an attack on a good man. Vinnie nevertheless has money at risk and requires the apprehension. Lula joins Stephanie in checking Mo's store, home, and familiar haunts, while Morelli warns that the weapon charge and disappearance deserve more attention than local sentiment allows.

Uncle Mo remains missing, and the Burg continues to close ranks against Stephanie. The case takes a darker direction when people connected to local drug activity are found dead. The victims do not fit the public image of Mo, but their appearance near the path of Stephanie's search makes it harder to treat his failure to appear as an isolated mistake. Ranger assists with dangerous apprehension work and Lula becomes increasingly active as Stephanie's partner. Joyce Barnhardt also enters the bounty business, turning routine recoveries into contests and adding interference when Stephanie already has difficulty getting witnesses to speak.

More bodies linked to the drug trade deepen the mystery around Mo's disappearance. Stephanie and Morelli compare what she learns through the bond search with what police know about the victims, although neither wants to yield control to the other. Mo's long-established reputation gives him protection: people assume a respected candy-store owner cannot belong in the same investigation as murdered dealers. Stephanie's searches and surveillance make her a target for intimidation, while Lula and Ranger provide backup. The evidence increasingly suggests that the fugitive and the killings are connected, but the motive and direction of that connection remain unresolved.

Stephanie narrows the search by looking past the neighborhood's stories about Uncle Mo and concentrating on his movements, weapon, and access. The dead dealers were not random obstacles to his flight; they form a pattern based on someone deciding who should be removed from the Burg. That pattern explains why fear and community loyalty have operated together to hide useful evidence. Morelli's police information and Ranger's operational help bring Stephanie closer to Mo, while Lula stays involved despite the growing risk. The hunt returns toward the familiar places where Mo's respectable identity was built and where he has been able to act without attracting suspicion.

Stephanie finds that Moses Bedemier is the killer behind the dead drug dealers. Uncle Mo has turned himself into a neighborhood vigilante, using his trusted public identity and the Burg's instinct to protect him as cover while deciding that murder is an acceptable way to remove the local drug trade. The concealed weapon that began the case was part of that secret life rather than an innocent lapse. Stephanie confronts Mo after the evidence closes around him. He responds with violence and dies in the final encounter, ending the killings and the bond pursuit. The result vindicates Stephanie's refusal to abandon the file, although neighbors must absorb the collapse of the harmless figure they defended. She completes the case with Lula established as a field partner and with continuing support from Ranger and Morelli.
